mainTopic: נידוי: who may impose it, how a sinning Torah scholar is treated, how a ban is released, and how powerful a ban is
overview: The גמרא proves from a ברייתא that a תלמיד who puts someone in נידוי for insulting him has a valid ban, and רב יוסף adds that a צורבא מרבנן may act on his own when the law is clear to him. Next comes a long story. רב יהודה bans a great scholar with a bad reputation, based on רבי יוחנן's teaching that one learns Torah only from a teacher who is like an angel of ה׳. After רב יהודה dies, the ban is not lifted, because of a קל וחומר from a ban made by רבי's maidservant. The scholar dies, and he is buried with the judges because he kept his sin private, as רבי אילעאי taught. The גמרא then tells the maidservant's story and the story of ריש לקיש, who wrongly banned a man over figs and needed the נשיא to release him. It brings different ways of handling a sinning Torah scholar: the אושא rule, ריש לקיש's view that he is never banned in public, מר זוטרא's practice, and רב פפא's use of lashes instead of a ban. Finally it explains the word שמתא, argues about whether a ban leaves a trace after it is lifted, and shows how powerful a ban is. The amud ends partway through רב יוסף's advice to a scholar who is afraid of a bully, and that advice continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A student's ostracism for his own honor is valid
steps.stepSummary: A תלמיד who placed someone in נידוי because that person insulted him has made a valid נידוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a student put someone in נידוי for the sake of his own honor, the נידוי counts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states a rule. A תלמיד who placed someone in נידוי because that person disrespected him has a real, binding נידוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person was not put in נידוי for a sin against Heaven. He was put in נידוי only for insulting the תלמיד. The rule is that this still counts. The next steps bring the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: A student, here a Torah scholar who is not yet at the level of his teacher
Placed under a ban; ostracism, where people keep their distance from the person
For his own honor, because someone insulted him

phrases.english: A student who ostracized someone for his own honor
his ostracism is a valid ostracism

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד's נידוי for an insult to his own honor is binding.

steps.title: A teaching about teacher and student
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא. A נידוי by the רב binds the תלמיד, but a נידוי by the תלמיד does not bind the רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: someone in נידוי by the teacher is in נידוי for the student. Someone in נידוי by the student is not in נידוי for the teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא as the source for the rule. This prepares the inference in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא is one-directional. The רב's נידוי binds the תלמיד. The תלמיד's נידוי does not bind the רב. The proof will come from what the ברייתא leaves unsaid.

keyTerms.meaning: A person who is under נידוי

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:
One ostracized by the teacher is ostracized for the student,
one ostracized by the student is not ostracized for the teacher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source for the rule in step 1
steps.raayaObject: The validity of a תלמיד's נידוי
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about נידוי between רב and תלמיד

steps.title: Inference: the student's ban binds everyone else
steps.stepSummary: Only the רב is excluded from keeping the תלמיד's נידוי. So everyone else must keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Only the teacher is not bound. That implies that for everyone else, he is in נידוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the ברייתא closely. Since only the רב is excluded, everyone else must treat the person as in נידוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This shows that a תלמיד's נידוי has real force over the general public. What is still missing is proof that this is about the תלמיד's own honor. That comes next.

phrases.english: It is only for the teacher that he is not ostracized,
which implies that for everyone else he is ostracized.

steps.raayaObject: That a תלמיד's נידוי binds the public
steps.raayaSupportSource: A careful reading of the ברייתא's wording

steps.title: Why was he banned? It cannot be for a sin
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ban in the ברייתא was for. It rules out a sin against Heaven, because then even the רב would have to keep the נידוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: For what was he put in נידוי? If it was for a matter of Heaven, the verse says: "There is no wisdom, no understanding and no counsel against ה׳"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what kind of נידוי the ברייתא means. It rules out one option to set up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose the person was banned for a sin. Then the רב's greater wisdom would not exempt him, because no wisdom stands against ה׳. So the רב's exemption must mean the ban was not about a sin.

keyTerms.meaning: Matters of Heaven, such as a sin against ה׳

phrases.english: For what was he ostracized?
If it was for matters of Heaven,
"There is no wisdom and no understanding
phrases.notes: משלי 21:30

phrases.english: and no counsel against the Lord"!

steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of נידוי is the ברייתא talking about?

steps.title: So it must be for the student's own honor
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא must be about a נידוי for the תלמיד's own honor. That proves the rule in step 1.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it about his own honor?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof. The ברייתא is about a ban for the תלמיד's own honor, and that ban binds everyone except the רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only a personal-honor ban explains why the רב is exempt. And since everyone else must keep the ban, a תלמיד's ban for his own honor is valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't it…? This introduces the only remaining option.

steps.whatToRemember: A תלמיד may put someone in נידוי for insulting him. That ban binds everyone except his own רב.

phrases.english: Rather, is it not for his own honor?

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא proves that a תלמיד's נידוי for his own honor is valid.

steps.title: A scholar may act on his own when the matter is clear
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף rules that a צורבא מרבנן may take the law into his own hands when he is sure of the ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: a young Torah scholar may carry out judgment for himself in a matter that is clear to him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives a related rule. A Torah scholar does not always need to go to בית דין first. When he is certain of the law, he may act on his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a new idea: a scholar may enforce the law himself, not only for his honor. The condition is that the matter be clear-cut to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A young Torah scholar, literally someone who is 'heated up' by Torah
That is clear and decided for him

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the rule that a scholar may act on his own, without בית דין, when the law is certain.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
A Torah scholar may execute judgment for himself
in a matter about which he is certain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the power of a scholar to act on his own
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A צורבא מרבנן may act on his own judgment when he is certain of the law.

steps.title: A scholar with a bad reputation: רב יהודה's dilemma
steps.stepSummary: A צורבא מרבנן had a bad reputation. רב יהודה was torn: the חכמים needed him, but leaving him alone would cause a חילול השם.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a Torah scholar with a bad reputation. רב יהודה said: what should we do? If we put him in שמתא, the חכמים need him. If we don't, the name of Heaven is desecrated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story. רב יהודה faces a hard choice about a great scholar with a bad name, and the next part will show what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two good values clash here. Banning him would lose a teacher the חכמים depend on. Not banning him would let a חילול השם continue.

keyTerms.meaning: His reputation was bad, literally 'what was heard about him was hated'
To put him in שמתא, a ban similar to נידוי
The name of Heaven is desecrated (חילול השם)

steps.confusionAlert: רב יהודה is not deciding yet. He is only laying out the problem, and the story continues in the next lines.

phrases.english: There was a certain Torah scholar
who had a bad reputation,
Rav Yehuda said: What should be done?
To excommunicate him: the Sages need him,

phrases.aramaic: לָא לְשַׁמְּתֵיהּ — קָא מִיתְּחִיל שְׁמָא דִשְׁמַיָּא.
phrases.english: not to excommunicate him: the name of Heaven is being desecrated.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן דַּהֲווֹ סְנוּ שׁוּמְעָנֵיהּ
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Should a needed scholar with a bad reputation be put in שמתא?

steps.title: רב יהודה asks for guidance
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה asks רבה בר בר חנה if he has heard any teaching about this kind of case.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to רבה בר בר חנה: Have you heard anything about this?
steps.whatsHappening: Since רב יהודה was stuck, he asks another scholar whether he knows any teaching on the matter. This line sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 7 left רב יהודה with two pulls: the חכמים need this scholar, but leaving him alone causes a חילול השם. Instead of deciding on his own, he looks for a received teaching to settle it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה:
phrases.english: He said to Rabba bar bar Chana:
phrases.notes: "He" is רב יהודה, who was torn about the case in the last step.

phrases.english: Have you heard anything about this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for a way out of the dilemma raised in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is there a known teaching about how to treat a needed scholar who has a bad reputation?

steps.title: Only learn Torah from a teacher who is like an angel
steps.stepSummary: Quoting רבי יוחנן on a פסוק in מלאכי, רבה בר בר חנה answers: learn Torah only from a רב who is like an angel of ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: רבי יוחנן said, what does the פסוק mean, "For the lips of the כהן keep knowledge, and they seek Torah from his mouth, for he is an angel of ה׳"? If the teacher is like an angel of ה׳, seek Torah from him. If not, do not seek Torah from him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה answers with a teaching of רבי יוחנן: a teacher's character matters, not just his knowledge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק links "seek Torah from his mouth" to "he is a מלאך of ה׳‎." רבי יוחנן reads this as a condition: only if the רב acts like an angel should people learn from him. So the claim that "the חכמים need him" does not protect a scholar who behaves badly.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of what is written?

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaching settles רב יהודה's dilemma from step 7: the need for the scholar's Torah does not outweigh his bad conduct.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: He said to him: Thus said Rabbi Yochanan:
What is the meaning of what is written:
"For the lips of the priest keep knowledge,
and they should seek Torah from his mouth,
for he is a messenger of the Lord of hosts."
phrases.notes: מלאכי 2:7. The word מלאך means both "messenger" and "angel," and the teaching builds on that.

phrases.english: If the teacher is like an angel of the Lord —
they should seek Torah from his mouth,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו — אַל יְבַקְּשׁוּ תּוֹרָה מִפִּיו.
phrases.english: and if not — they should not seek Torah from his mouth.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a teaching in step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A teacher who does not act like an angel of ה׳ should not be learned from, so his being needed is not a reason to spare him.

steps.title: רב יהודה places the scholar in נידוי
steps.stepSummary: Relying on רבי יוחנן's teaching, רב יהודה puts the scholar in נידוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה placed him in נידוי.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה makes his decision: he bans the scholar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching removed the reason to hold back. The חכמים no longer need to learn from this scholar, so preventing חילול השם wins.

keyTerms.meaning: He placed him in נידוי (a ban)

steps.whatToRemember: A scholar's Torah knowledge does not shield him from נידוי if his conduct causes a חילול השם.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda placed him under a ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Acts on the teaching given in step 9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב יהודה bans the scholar despite the חכמים needing him.

steps.title: רב יהודה falls ill and laughs when he sees the scholar
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה becomes sick. The חכמים visit him, the banned scholar comes along, and רב יהודה laughs when he sees him.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end רב יהודה became weak. The חכמים came to visit him, and that scholar came with them. When רב יהודה saw him, he laughed.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves forward to רב יהודה's final illness. His laughter sets up the scholar's complaint in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even while still banned, the scholar joins the visit. רב יהודה's laughter is puzzling, and the next two steps explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: To ask about his health (to visit him)

phrases.english: In the end, Rav Yehuda became ill.
The Rabbis came to visit him,
and he also came along with them,
phrases.notes: "He" is the banned scholar.

phrases.english: when Rav Yehuda saw him, he laughed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story after the ban.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: the dying רב יהודה laughs on seeing the banned scholar.

steps.title: The scholar complains about the laughter
steps.stepSummary: The scholar protests: it was not enough to ban me, now you laugh at me too?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Wasn't it enough that you banned that man, but you laugh at me too?!
steps.whatsHappening: The banned scholar challenges רב יהודה, feeling mocked on top of being banned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scholar takes the laughter as a personal insult added to the ban. This complaint pushes רב יהודה to explain why he laughed.

phrases.english: He said to him: Was it not enough
that you banned that man,
phrases.notes: "That man" is a polite way of saying "me." He is talking about himself.

phrases.english: but you also laugh at me?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to רב יהודה's laughter in step 11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Laughing at someone you already banned looks like needless mockery.

steps.title: רב יהודה explains: I am happy I did not flatter
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says he was not laughing at the scholar. He is happy to leave the world knowing he never flattered even a man as important as him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am not laughing at you. I am laughing because I am going to the next world happy that I did not flatter even a man like you.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the complaint: the laughter was joy about his own honesty, not mockery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Banning a great scholar was hard, and flattering him would have been easier. רב יהודה is glad he stood firm, and this gives him peace as he dies.

keyTerms.meaning: That world, the World to Come
My mind is at ease and happy

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a judge or רב must not favor a person just because he is important.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am not laughing at you,
rather, that as I go to that world
my mind is happy,
that even to a man like you
I did not show flattery.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the scholar's complaint in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the act: the laughter was joy, not mockery.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יהודה was mocking the banned scholar.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was rejoicing that he judged honestly without flattering a great man.

steps.title: After רב יהודה dies, the scholar asks to be released
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה dies. The scholar comes to the בית מדרש and asks the חכמים to lift his ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה died. The scholar came to the בית מדרש and said to them: Release me!
steps.whatsHappening: With רב יהודה gone, the scholar asks the חכמים to undo the נידוי. This sets up their reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the person who imposed a נידוי is the one to lift it. Since רב יהודה has died, the scholar asks someone else to do it.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda passed away.
He came to the study hall,
he said to them: Release me!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The story moves past רב יהודה's death to the question of lifting the ban.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Will the חכמים release him from the ban now that רב יהודה is gone?

steps.title: The Sages: only someone as great as רב יהודה can release you
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים say no one here is as great as רב יהודה, so they send the scholar to רבי יהודה נשיאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים said to him: There is no one here as great as רב יהודה who could release you. Instead, go to רבי יהודה נשיאה so that he can release you.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים refuse to lift the ban themselves and send the scholar to the נשיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lifting a ban needs someone of at least the same standing as the one who imposed it. Since nobody in the בית מדרש matches רב יהודה, they send him to the leader of the generation.

keyTerms.meaning: The נשיא (head of the Jewish community) in ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: The Rabbis said to him:
A man as important as Rav Yehuda
is not here who could release you,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא זִיל לְגַבֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה
phrases.english: rather, go to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
so that he can release you.

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבְרָא דַּחֲשִׁיב כְּרַב יְהוּדָה לֵיכָּא הָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request in step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No one here is great enough to release a ban imposed by רב יהודה. Go to רבי יהודה נשיאה.

steps.title: רבי יהודה נשיאה sends רבי אמי to examine the case
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה נשיאה tells רבי אמי to look into the case and release the scholar if it is right to do so.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went before him. He said to רבי אמי: Go out and examine his case. If he needs to be released, release him.
steps.whatsHappening: The scholar reaches רבי יהודה נשיאה, who hands the case to רבי אמי to investigate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה נשיאה does not lift the ban automatically. He asks for a real check of whether release is deserved, and he gives רבי אמי authority to act for him.

phrases.english: He went before him,
he said to Rabbi Ami:
phrases.notes: Here the speaker is רבי יהודה נשיאה.

phrases.english: Go out and examine his case,
if it is necessary to release him —
release him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the חכמים's instruction in step 15 to go to רבי יהודה נשיאה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה נשיאה tells רבי אמי to check the case and release the ban only if it is warranted.

steps.title: רבי אמי reviews the case and leans toward lifting the ban
steps.stepSummary: Following רבי יהודה נשיאה's instruction, רבי אמי examines the case and thinks to release the scholar.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אמי looked into his case and thought to release him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אמי does what he was told and studies the scholar's case. He leans toward lifting the ban, which sets up the objection that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the first sign that the ban might end. The word סבר shows it was only his first thought, not a final decision. That leaves room for the challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: He thought, he was inclined to

phrases.english: Rabbi Ami looked into his case,
and he thought to release him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the instruction רבי יהודה נשיאה gave in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אמי's first leaning is to lift the ban.

steps.title: רבי שמואל בר נחמני objects with a קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני argues that even a ban from רבי's maidservant was respected for three years, so the ban of רב יהודה certainly must be.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני stood up and said: If the חכמים did not treat lightly the ban of a maidservant of רבי's house for three years, how much more so must they respect the ban of יהודה our colleague.
steps.whatsHappening: Someone stands up to block the release. He argues that a ban by a great sage like רב יהודה must not be cancelled easily.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses a קל וחומר, an argument from a smaller case to a bigger one. If the חכמים honored a ban made by a maidservant for three years, a ban made by a great חכם like רב יהודה deserves at least as much respect. This directly attacks רבי אמי's leaning to release the scholar.

keyTerms.meaning: He stood up on his feet (to speak strongly)
A ban; a person in נידוי is kept apart from the community
How much more so (the wording of a קל וחומר)

phrases.aramaic: עָמַד רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי עַל רַגְלָיו וְאָמַר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani stood up on his feet and said:
If the maidservant of the house of Rabbi,
the Sages did not treat lightly
her ban, for three years,
phrases.notes: "Her ban" means a ban she placed on someone else.

phrases.aramaic: יְהוּדָה חֲבֵירֵינוּ עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה.
phrases.english: then Yehuda our colleague, all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה שִׁפְחָה שֶׁל בֵּית רַבִּי לֹא נָהֲגוּ חֲכָמִים קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי אמי's leaning to release the scholar.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אמי's thought to lift the ban
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר: if a maidservant's ban was respected for three years, a great sage's ban must be respected even more.

steps.title: רבי זירא sees the elder's rare visit as a sign
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא notes that this elder had not come to the בית מדרש for years, and his arriving now shows the scholar should not be released.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא said: Why did this elder come to the study hall today, when he has not come for many years? Learn from this that we should not release him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא backs up the objection. He reads the elder's unexpected visit as a sign that the ban should stay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The support here does not come from logic but from timing. The elder hardly ever comes, yet he showed up just when this case was being decided. רבי זירא concludes this is no accident, so the answer is not to release him.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not right, one should not

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said:
What is behind what we see here, that he came today,
this elder, to the study hall,
when for many years he has not come?

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לָא מִיבְּעֵי לְמִישְׁרֵא לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Learn from this that he should not be released.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ לָא מִיבְּעֵי לְמִישְׁרֵא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי שמואל בר נחמני's objection with a sign.
steps.raayaObject: That the ban should not be lifted
steps.raayaSupportSource: The unusual timing of the elder's visit after many years away

steps.title: The ban stays and the scholar leaves crying
steps.stepSummary: רבי אמי does not release him, and the scholar leaves in tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did not release him. He went out crying as he went.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the decision: the ban is not lifted. The scholar leaves the בית מדרש crying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection in step 18 and the sign in step 19 win out over רבי אמי's first leaning. The scholar's hope of being released is now over.

phrases.english: He did not release him.
He went out, crying as he went.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the result of the debate over releasing him.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ban of רב יהודה stays in place.

steps.title: The scholar dies and only the judges' cave accepts him
steps.stepSummary: A wasp stings the scholar and he dies. The cave of the pious will not accept him for burial, but the cave of the judges does.
steps.simpleTranslation: A wasp came and stung him on his private part, and he died. They brought him to the cave of the pious, and it did not accept him. They brought him to the cave of the judges, and it accepted him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story tells how the scholar died and where he was buried. This sets up the question in the next step: why did the judges' cave accept him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being turned away from the cave of the חסידים shows he was not counted among the pious. Yet being accepted by the cave of the judges shows he still had some merit, and the גמרא will explain what it was.

phrases.english: A wasp came and stung him on his private part, and he died.
They brought him into the cave of the pious
and it did not accept him.
They brought him into the cave of the judges
and it accepted him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story after the scholar leaves.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He was refused burial among the pious but accepted among the judges.

steps.title: Why was he accepted at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why this scholar was accepted into the cave of the judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops the story to ask a question. It wants to know why a man who sinned was still accepted for burial with the judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being turned away from the cave of the pious makes sense, since he sinned. The puzzle is the honor he still received. The answer will show what merit he had.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the burial outcome in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the cave of the judges accepted him despite his sin

steps.title: He followed רבי אילעאי and never shamed God's name in public
steps.stepSummary: He was accepted because he acted like רבי אילעאי taught: a person overcome by his inclination should go where no one knows him, wear black, and if he still sins, at least not desecrate God's name in public.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he acted like רבי אילעאי. As it is taught: רבי אילעאי says: If a person sees that his evil inclination is overpowering him, he should go to a place where no one knows him, wear black and wrap himself in black, and do what his heart desires, and not desecrate the name of Heaven in public.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting a ברייתא from רבי אילעאי. The scholar sinned only in private, away from people who knew him, so he did not cause a public חילול השם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אילעאי gives steps for a person losing his fight with the יצר הרע: leave for a place where he is unknown and dress in black like a mourner. If he still sins, the sin stays private and God's name is not shamed in public. Because the scholar kept his sin private, he kept enough merit to be buried with the judges.

keyTerms.meaning: Desecrate the name of Heaven (חילול השם)

steps.whatToRemember: The scholar lost the burial honor of the pious but was still buried with the judges, because he kept his sin private and avoided a public חילול השם, as רבי אילעאי taught.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי אילעאי is not giving permission to sin. His main point is that a sin should never become a public חילול השם.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how much weight the גמרא gives to avoiding public חילול השם, even for someone who has failed in private.

phrases.english: Because he acted like Rabbi Ilai.
As it is taught: Rabbi Ilai says:

phrases.aramaic: אִם רוֹאֶה אָדָם שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו —
phrases.english: If a person sees that his inclination is overpowering him,
he should go to a place where no one knows him,
and wear black and wrap himself in black,
and do what his heart desires,
and not desecrate the name of Heaven in public.

steps.triggerLanguage: דַּעֲבַד כְּרַבִּי אִילְעַאי. דְּתַנְיָא, רַבִּי אִילְעַאי אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He sinned only in private, following רבי אילעאי, and so avoided a public חילול השם. That merit earned him burial with the judges.

steps.title: What was the story of the maidservant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the details of the story about the maidservant in רבי's house.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the story of the maidservant of רבי's house?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next story. It asks what happened with the maidservant of רבי's house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A story about this maidservant was referred to earlier without details. Now the גמרא stops to ask for the full story, which comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The household of רבי יהודה הנשיא
What is it? (asking for the details of something mentioned)

phrases.aramaic: שִׁפְחָה שֶׁל בֵּית רַבִּי מַאי הִיא?
phrases.english: What is the story of the maidservant of Rabbi's house?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the maidservant story that רבי שמואל בר נחמני cited in step 18 and asks for its details.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The details of the maidservant's story.

steps.title: The maidservant bans a man who hit his grown son
steps.stepSummary: The maidservant saw a man hitting his adult son. She put him in שמתא for breaking לפני עור לא תתן מכשול.
steps.simpleTranslation: The maidservant of רבי's house saw a man hitting his grown son. She said: Let that man be in שמתא, because he is breaking 'Do not put a stumbling block before the blind.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells the story. The maidservant banned a man because he was hitting his grown-up son.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She did not ban him just for being harsh. She banned him because he was breaking a specific פסוק. Hitting a grown son sets him up to sin, so it counts as putting a stumbling block in front of him.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not put a stumbling block before the blind

phrases.english: That the maidservant of Rabbi's house
saw a certain man
who was hitting his grown son.
She said: Let that man be under a ban,
because he is transgressing
"Before a blind person do not place a stumbling block."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:14

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: She banned a man who hit his adult son, for breaking לפני עור.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the פסוק is about hitting a grown son
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא confirms that לפני עור includes hitting one's grown son.
steps.simpleTranslation: As was taught: 'Do not put a stumbling block before the blind.' The פסוק is talking about someone who hits his grown son.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that the maidservant had a real source for what she said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads the פסוק as covering a father who hits his grown son. This backs up the maidservant's reason for the ban, so it was not just her own feeling.

phrases.english: As it is taught: "Before a blind person do not place a stumbling block" —
the verse is speaking about one who hits his grown son.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the maidservant's reasoning.
steps.raayaObject: The maidservant's claim that hitting a grown son breaks לפני עור.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא explaining the פסוק in ויקרא.

steps.title: ריש לקיש bans a man who ate figs
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש was guarding an orchard. A man ate figs and ignored his shouting, so ריש לקיש put him in שמתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש was guarding an orchard. A man came and ate figs. ריש לקיש shouted at him, but he ignored him. ריש לקיש said: Let that man be in שמתא.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts. ריש לקיש bans a man who is eating figs from the orchard he is guarding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ban is not for breaking a תורה rule like in the last story. It is over a money matter, eating someone else's figs. This difference becomes the key point in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised his voice at him (shouted)
He paid no attention to him

phrases.english: Reish Lakish was guarding an orchard.
A certain man came and was eating figs.
He raised his voice at him,
but he paid no attention to him.
He said: Let that man be under a ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another story about placing a ban, this time over a money matter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש places a ban on a man who ate figs he was guarding.

steps.title: The man bans ריש לקיש right back
steps.stepSummary: The man argues that owing money does not make someone deserve a ban, and he bans ריש לקיש instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man said to him: On the contrary, let that man (you) be in שמתא! Even if I owe you money, do I deserve a נידוי from you?
steps.whatsHappening: The man pushes back against ריש לקיש's ban. He says a money debt is no reason for a ban, and he bans ריש לקיש himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man makes a clear distinction: eating the figs makes him owe money, not deserve a נידוי. Because ריש לקיש banned someone who did not deserve it, the man claims the ban should land on ריש לקיש.

keyTerms.meaning: A ban; being set apart from the community

phrases.english: He said to him: On the contrary,
let that man be under a ban!
phrases.notes: Here 'that man' means ריש לקיש himself. It is a polite way of not saying 'you.'

phrases.english: If I became obligated to you for money,
did I become obligated to you for a ban?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ban ריש לקיש placed in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's ban on the fig-eater.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A money debt makes you owe payment, not a ban. So a ban for it is wrong.

steps.title: The בית מדרש rules: his ban counts, yours does not
steps.stepSummary: The scholars rule that the man's ban on ריש לקיש is valid, and ריש לקיש's ban on the man is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: He came to the בית מדרש. They said to him: His ban is a ban. Yours is not a ban.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש asks the scholars, and they rule in favor of the man who ate the figs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The scholars accept the man's argument. A money matter does not justify a ban, so ריש לקיש's ban has no effect. Because ריש לקיש banned someone who did not deserve it, the man's ban on him does take effect.

phrases.english: He came to the study hall.
They said to him: His is a ban,
yours is not a ban.

steps.confusionAlert: Even a great scholar like ריש לקיש did not have a valid ban here. A ban must have a proper reason, and owing money is not one.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules on the dispute between ריש לקיש and the man.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A ban over a simple money debt is not valid. A ban against someone who banned without cause is valid.

steps.title: How can ריש לקיש fix this?
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש asks how he can get out of the ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is his fix?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that ריש לקיש is under a valid ban, the question is how he can be released. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the ban is ruled valid, the story turns practical. The question is how to undo it.

phrases.english: And what is his remedy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the ruling that ריש לקיש is under a valid ban.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to be released from the ban.

steps.title: Go to the man to be released
steps.stepSummary: The scholars tell ריש לקיש to go to the man so he can release the ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: Go to him so that he releases you.
steps.whatsHappening: The first answer is simple: the person who placed the ban can lift it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual way out of a ban is for the one who placed it to release it. So ריש לקיש is told to find the man.

phrases.english: Go to him so that he may release you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The one who placed the ban can release it.

steps.title: But I don't know who he is
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש points out that he does not know the man, so he cannot find him.
steps.simpleTranslation: I do not know him.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש raises a practical problem with the answer: the man is a stranger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first fix depends on finding the man who placed the ban. Since ריש לקיש cannot identify him, a different solution is needed.

phrases.english: I do not know him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the answer of step 31 cannot work here.
steps.kashyaTarget: The advice to go to the man who placed the ban.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: You cannot ask someone to release you if you do not know who he is.

steps.title: Go to the נשיא instead
steps.stepSummary: The scholars tell ריש לקיש to go to the נשיא, who can release the ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Go to the נשיא so that he releases you.
steps.whatsHappening: The scholars give a backup solution: the נשיא can release the ban.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the person who placed the ban cannot be found, the leader of the generation has the power to lift it.

keyTerms.meaning: The נשיא, leader of the Jewish community

phrases.english: They said to him: Go to the Nasi
so that he may release you,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Solves the problem raised in step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The נשיא can release the ban.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the נשיא releases an unknown ban
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if you do not know who banned you, the נשיא can release the ban.
steps.simpleTranslation: As was taught: If someone was banned and does not know who banned him, he should go to the נשיא, and the נשיא releases his ban.
steps.whatsHappening: The scholars back up their advice with a ברייתא that covers exactly this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא deals with someone who does not know who banned him. That is ריש לקיש's exact situation, so it proves the נשיא is the right address.
steps.whatToRemember: A ban needs a proper reason. Owing money is not enough, and an improper ban can come back on the one who placed it. To be released, go to the one who banned you. If you do not know who he is, go to the נשיא.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא: נִידּוּהוּ וְאֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ מִי נִידָּהוּ,
phrases.english: As it is taught: If they banned him and he does not know who banned him,
he should go to the Nasi,
and he will release his ban for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the advice in step 33.
steps.raayaObject: The advice that the נשיא can release ריש לקיש's ban.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about someone banned by an unknown person.

steps.title: The אושא enactment: a sinning אב בית דין is first sent home, not banned
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא reports that in אושא they ruled: an אב בית דין who sins is not banned but told to stay home. If he sins again, he is banned because of חילול השם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: In אושא they made a rule. If the head of the court sins, we do not put him in נידוי. Instead we tell him, "Keep your honor and stay at home." If he sins again, we do put him in נידוי, because otherwise there would be a חילול השם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a rule from אושא about how to treat an אב בית דין who sins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first time, his honor is protected: he is quietly told to step back instead of being banned. If he sins a second time, protecting him would itself cause a חילול השם, because people would think important people get away with sin. So he is banned.

keyTerms.meaning: Head of the court, second in rank to the נשיא

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main question of the section: how to balance respect for Torah leaders against the need to hold them accountable.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
In Usha they enacted:
A head of the court who sinned
they do not ban him,
rather, one says to him:
"Keep your honor and stay in your home."
phrases.notes: מלכים ב 14:10

phrases.english: If he went back and sinned again
they ban him,
because of the desecration of God's name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the story of ריש לקיש's ban to a new topic: banning important Torah figures.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אב בית דין who sins is told to stay home the first time. If he sins again, he is banned because of חילול השם.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: a Torah scholar is never banned in public
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that ריש לקיש disagrees. In his view a sinning תלמיד חכם is not banned publicly, based on the פסוק about the prophet stumbling 'at night'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with ריש לקיש. ריש לקיש said: If a תלמיד חכם sins, we do not ban him in public. The פסוק says, "You will stumble in the day, and the prophet will also stumble with you at night." This teaches us to cover up his sin like the night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that ריש לקיש holds differently from the אושא rule, and it quotes his view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the אושא rule, a repeat sinner is banned openly. ריש לקיש says a Torah scholar is never banned in public, even then. He reads 'night' in the פסוק as a hint that a great person's failing should be kept hidden.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Reish Lakish.
For Reish Lakish said:
A Torah scholar who sinned
they do not ban him in public,
as it is said:
"And you shall stumble in the day,
and the prophet too shall stumble with you at night"
phrases.notes: הושע 4:5

phrases.english: Cover him up like the night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows an opposing view to the אושא rule from step 35.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sinning תלמיד חכם is never banned in public; his sin is kept hidden.

steps.title: מר זוטרא banned himself before banning a scholar
steps.stepSummary: Whenever מר זוטרא חסידא had to ban a young scholar, he first banned himself and then the scholar. At home he released himself first and then the scholar.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a young Torah scholar deserved a ban, מר זוטרא the Pious would first ban himself and then ban the scholar. When he came back to his lodging, he would release himself and then release the scholar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how one pious sage handled banning a Torah scholar while still respecting him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By banning himself together with the scholar, מר זוטרא showed respect for the scholar's Torah and softened his shame. He released himself and the scholar quickly, so the ban served to discipline, not to humiliate.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra the Pious,
when a young Torah scholar became liable for a ban,
first he would ban himself,
and then he would ban him.
When he would enter his lodging,
he would release himself,
and then he would release him.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא חֲסִידָא, כִּי מִיחַיַּיב צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן שַׁמְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example of banning a scholar in a way that protects his honor.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מר זוטרא banned himself before banning a scholar, and released himself before releasing the scholar.

steps.title: A scholar may ban and release himself
steps.stepSummary: רב גידל in the name of רב rules that a תלמיד חכם may put himself in נידוי and may release himself from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב גידל said in the name of רב: A Torah scholar may ban himself, and he may release himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the rule that explains how מר זוטרא could ban and release himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We saw in steps 31-34 that normally only the person who banned you, or the נשיא, can release you. This rule shows that a self-imposed ban is different: the scholar who placed it can lift it himself, with no one else needed.

phrases.english: Rav Giddel said that Rav said:
A Torah scholar may ban himself,
and may release himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the legal basis for מר זוטרא's practice in step 37.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A תלמיד חכם can place a ban on himself and lift it himself.

steps.title: רב פפא praises himself for never banning a scholar
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says he deserves reward because he never banned a Torah scholar.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Let good come to me, because I never banned a Torah scholar.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא shares his personal practice. It sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His statement goes further than the earlier steps. Those steps protected a scholar's honor while still banning him; רב פפא avoided banning scholars at all. This raises an obvious question: what did he do when a scholar really deserved it?

keyTerms.meaning: Let (reward) come to me; I deserve credit

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Let good come to me,
for I have never banned a young Torah scholar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a sage who avoided banning scholars entirely.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב פפא never banned a Torah scholar.

steps.title: What did רב פפא do when a scholar deserved a ban?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב פפא handled a scholar who deserved a ban, since he never banned one.
steps.simpleTranslation: But when a Torah scholar did deserve a ban, what would he do?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about רב פפא's statement. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Scholars surely sometimes deserved discipline. So the גמרא wants to know what רב פפא used instead of a ban.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא כִּי קָא מִיחַיַּיב צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן שַׁמְתָּא,
phrases.english: But when a young Torah scholar was liable for a ban,
what would he do?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא כִּי קָא מִיחַיַּיב צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן שַׁמְתָּא, הֵיכִי עָבֵיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how רב פפא's practice worked in real life.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What discipline רב פפא used for a scholar who deserved a ban.

steps.title: Like in ארץ ישראל: lashes instead of a ban
steps.stepSummary: He followed the practice of the מערבא, where they would set up a court to give a scholar lashes but not to ban him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He did as they do in the מערבא (ארץ ישראל): there they appoint a court to give a Torah scholar lashes, but they do not appoint a court to ban him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: רב פפא gave lashes instead of a ban, following the custom of ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ban lasts a long time and publicly cuts the scholar off from people. That hurts the honor of Torah more than lashes do. So the scholar was still disciplined, but in a way that ends quickly.
steps.whatToRemember: Different approaches to a sinning scholar: the אושא rule (stay home first, ban if he sins again), ריש לקיש (never ban him publicly), מר זוטרא (ban yourself along with him), and רב פפא and the מערבא (lashes instead of a ban). All of them try to discipline the scholar without shaming the Torah.

phrases.english: Like that which they do in the West:
phrases.notes: "The West" is ארץ ישראל, which lies west of בבל.

phrases.english: they appoint a court for lashes for a young Torah scholar,
but they do not appoint a court for a ban.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 40.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He gave lashes instead of a ban, following the practice of ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: What does the word for a ban mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the word שמתא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of the word שמתא (a ban)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by asking what the word שמתא stands for. It is setting up the answers of רב and שמואל that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last few steps were about when to put a scholar in נידוי. Now the גמרא explains why a ban is so serious by breaking down the word itself.

keyTerms.meaning: A ban, the formal shunning of a person by בית דין

phrases.english: What is [the meaning of the word] shamta?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from practical stories about banning scholars to the meaning of the word for a ban
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning behind the word שמתא

steps.title: רב: the word means 'there is death'
steps.stepSummary: רב explains שמתא as two words joined together: שם מיתה, 'there is death'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: שמתא means 'there is death'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers that שמתא is made of two words, שם (there) and מיתה (death).
steps.deeperAnalysis: By reading death into the word, רב shows how severe a ban is. Being banned is described as a kind of death.

phrases.english: Rav said: 'There is death.'
phrases.notes: He is splitting שמתא into שם + מיתה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the question of step 42
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שמתא = שם מיתה, there is death

steps.title: שמואל: the word means 'he will be a desolation', and it sticks
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains שמתא as שממה יהיה, and adds that the ban clings to a person like grease absorbed in an oven.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: שמתא means 'he will be a desolation', and it affects him like grease smeared on an oven.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל gives a different reading of the word: the banned person will become a desolation. He adds a picture: the ban soaks into him like grease into an oven wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grease rubbed on an oven never fully comes out. In the same way, part of the ban's curse stays with the person even after the ban is lifted. This detail sets up the next step.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: 'He will be a desolation,'
and it is effective on him like fat [smeared] on an oven.
phrases.notes: The point is that grease soaks into the oven wall and some always stays behind.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to step 42, plus the idea that the ban leaves a lasting mark
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שמתא = שממה יהיה, and the ban leaves a lasting trace like grease in an oven

steps.title: ריש לקיש: the ban leaves completely, from all 248 limbs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that שמואל's grease picture argues with ריש לקיש, who says the ban leaves fully from all 248 limbs, just as it entered them all.
steps.simpleTranslation: This argues with ריש לקיש, who said: just as the ban enters all 248 limbs, so when it leaves, it leaves from all 248 limbs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a disagreement. ריש לקיש holds that when a ban is lifted, nothing of it remains.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said part of the ban stays behind, like grease. ריש לקיש says the ban goes out exactly as fully as it came in, through all 248 limbs of the body. So the two disagree about whether lifting a ban fully cleans the person.

keyTerms.meaning: Limbs or organs of the body
248, the traditional number of limbs in the body

phrases.english: And it disagrees with Reish Lakish.
For Reish Lakish said:

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁנִּכְנֶסֶת בְּמָאתַיִם וְאַרְבָּעִים וּשְׁמוֹנָה אֵיבָרִים,
phrases.english: Just as it enters the two hundred and forty-eight limbs,
phrases.notes: 'It' means the ban.

phrases.english: so too when it leaves,
it leaves from the two hundred and forty-eight limbs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that שמואל's 'grease' idea conflicts with another אמורא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ban leaves a person completely when lifted, just as it entered every limb

steps.title: Hints from the גימטריא of חרם and רחם
steps.stepSummary: Support for ריש לקיש: חרם (a ban) and רחם (mercy) both add up to 248, so the ban enters all limbs, and mercy removes it from all limbs.
steps.simpleTranslation: When it enters, as the פסוק says 'And the city shall be חרם', and חרם adds up to 248. When it leaves, as the פסוק says 'In anger remember רחם (mercy)', and רחם also adds up to 248.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two פסוקים whose key words have the number value 248, to back up ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חרם (ח=8, ר=200, ם=40) equals 248, hinting that a ban fills all 248 limbs. רחם has the same letters and the same value, hinting that when mercy lifts the ban, it leaves all 248 limbs. Nothing stays behind.

keyTerms.meaning: A ban or curse, a stronger form of נידוי
The number value of a word's letters

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל: a ban leaves a trace even after it is lifted (grease in an oven). ריש לקיש: it leaves completely from all 248 limbs (חרם = רחם = 248).

phrases.english: When it enters, as it is written:
'And the city shall be ḥerem'
phrases.notes: יהושע 6:17

phrases.english: and ḥerem in gematria is two hundred and forty-eight.
When it leaves, as it is written:
'In anger remember mercy (raḥem)'
phrases.notes: חבקוק 3:2

phrases.english: and raḥem in gematria is the same amount.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֶׁהִיא נִכְנֶסֶת, דִּכְתִיב: וְהָיְתָה הָעִיר חֵרֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives scriptural hints supporting ריש לקיש's statement
steps.raayaObject: ריש לקיש's claim that a ban enters and leaves all 248 limbs
steps.raayaSupportSource: Gematria of חרם (יהושע 6:17) and רחם (חבקוק 3:2), both equal 248

steps.title: רב יוסף: a ban works even on a dog's tail
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that if you throw a ban even on a dog's tail, it will do its harm.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: Throw a ban on a dog's tail, and it will do its work.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives a strong statement about how powerful a ban is. It works even on an animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds a new point to the discussion of a ban's severity. Its power does not depend on the target being a person who understands it.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
Cast a ban on the tail of a dog
and it will do its own work.
phrases.notes: 'It' is the ban: it will still cause harm.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: שְׁדִי שַׁמְתָּא אַגְּנוּבְתָּא דְכַלְבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of a ban's power with a new, striking claim
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ban takes effect even on an animal

steps.title: The story of the dog that ate the רבנן's shoes
steps.stepSummary: A dog was eating the shoes of the רבנן. Not knowing who did it, they put the culprit under a ban, and the dog's tail caught fire and burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a dog that kept eating the shoes of the רבנן, and they did not know who was doing it, so they banned the culprit. Fire caught on the dog's tail and burned it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows רב יוסף's statement really happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן did not even know the culprit was a dog. They banned whoever it was, and the punishment landed on the dog's tail. This shows a ban works even on an animal, just as רב יוסף said.
steps.whyThisMatters: The story backs up the whole סוגיא's point: a ban is extremely powerful, which is why the רבנן were so careful about using it on Torah scholars.

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָהוּא כַּלְבָּא דַּהֲוָה אָכֵיל מְסָאנֵי דְרַבָּנַן
phrases.english: For there was a certain dog that would eat the shoes of the Sages
and they did not know who it was,
and they banned him.
phrases.notes: They banned whoever was doing it, not knowing it was a dog.

phrases.english: Fire caught on its tail and consumed it.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהָהוּא כַּלְבָּא דַּהֲוָה אָכֵיל מְסָאנֵי דְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A story that shows רב יוסף's statement in action
steps.raayaObject: רב יוסף's claim that a ban works even on a dog
steps.raayaSupportSource: The story of the dog that ate the רבנן's shoes and had its tail burned

steps.title: A violent man harasses a young scholar, and רב יוסף says to ban him
steps.stepSummary: A violent man was troubling a צורבא מרבנן. The scholar went to רב יוסף, who told him to go and ban the man.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a violent man who was causing suffering to a young Torah scholar. The scholar came before רב יוסף. רב יוסף said to him: Go and put him under a ban.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story about a ban, right after the dog story. It sets up the problem: a bully is hurting a scholar, and רב יוסף's first advice is to ban him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same רב יוסף who taught that a ban works even on a dog's tail (Step 47). So it makes sense that his advice is to use a ban. The rest of the story shows how the scholar handles his fear.

keyTerms.meaning: A violent, strong-armed person; a bully
Go and put him under a ban

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא אַלָּמָא דַּהֲוָה קָא מְצַעַר לֵיהּ
phrases.english: There was a certain violent man who was causing suffering
to a certain young Torah scholar.
He came before Rav Yosef.
He said to him: Go and put him under a ban.
phrases.notes: "He said" here is רב יוסף, giving advice to the scholar.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא אַלָּמָא דַּהֲוָה קָא מְצַעַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about the power of a ban, after the dog story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף advises a harassed scholar to put the bully under a ban.

steps.title: The scholar is afraid to ban the bully
steps.stepSummary: The scholar objects to the advice: he is afraid of the violent man.
steps.simpleTranslation: The scholar said to him: I am afraid of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The scholar pushes back against רב יוסף's advice. He is scared the bully will hurt him even more if he bans him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not a question about whether a ban works. It is a practical problem: banning a dangerous man openly could make things worse for the scholar.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am afraid of him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Objects to רב יוסף's advice in Step 49.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's advice to ban the bully.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Banning a violent man openly puts the scholar in danger.

steps.title: רב יוסף suggests a written ban
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers the fear by suggesting a written ban document against the man.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said to him: Take out a written ban against him.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף tries to solve the scholar's fear with a different method: a written ban instead of a spoken one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is that the scholar would not have to face the bully and say the ban to him in person. A document could do the job instead.

phrases.english: He said to him: Take out a written ban against him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the scholar's fear from Step 50.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban must be said to the bully's face, which is dangerous.
steps.terutzMaskana: A written ban could be used instead of speaking it directly.

steps.title: The scholar is even more afraid of a written ban
steps.stepSummary: The scholar says a written ban makes him even more afraid.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the more so I am afraid of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The scholar rejects the written-ban idea too. He feels it would make his fear even worse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A written ban is public and lasting, so the bully would certainly find out and come after him. So the second suggestion seems worse than the first.

phrases.english: All the more so I am afraid of him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the written-ban suggestion of Step 51.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion of a written ban.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A written ban is even more public, so it is even more dangerous.

steps.title: רב יוסף says to put the written ban in a jug
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף gives a quieter method: take the written ban and place it inside a jug. The instructions continue in the next part of the story.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Take it and put it down into a jug,
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף starts giving a hidden way to ban the man, so the bully will not find out. The sentence is not finished here; the story continues with the next instructions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Hiding the written ban in a jug solves the fear: no one sees it, yet it still has power. This fits רב יוסף's teaching that a ban does its harm no matter what (Step 47).

phrases.english: He said to him: Take it,
put it down into a jug,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the scholar's increased fear from Step 52.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Hidden method of performing the ban
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A written ban must be made public, which is too dangerous.
steps.terutzMaskana: The written ban can be hidden in a jug, so the bully will not know.
